content: Randomized studies that included a single group were analyzed, and the pooled proportion of an event, along with confidence intervals, was calculated using the generic inverse variance method. For continuous outcomes, either a mean difference or a standardized mean difference was calculated, particularly when studies employed different scales to measure the same outcome. When feasible, forest plots from the meta-analyses were provided to the Guideline Development Group (GDG). For outcomes that could not be quantitatively synthesized, results were either presented as median effects with interquartile ranges or described narratively based on the direction of the effect or statistical significance as reported in the primary studies. The software RevMan, developed by the Nordic Cochrane Center, was used for these analyses. Studies on patient values, preferences, acceptability, equity, and feasibility were identified through two methods. First, during the screening of studies on treatment effects and costs, two investigators identified potentially relevant studies in these areas. Second, a separate search was conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO databases from January 2000 to July 2015. Keywords related to sexually transmitted infections (STIs) were combined with terms such as preference, adherence, satisfaction, attitudes, health utilities, value, equity, and feasibility. This search yielded 2,563 unique references, of which 162 studies were selected for full-text review. Any study design addressing equity or feasibility was included. Additionally, adherence data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or non-randomized studies were collected, synthesized, and presented in evidence profiles for each PICO question. Patient utility and health status value studies examined how patients value alternative health states and their experiences with treatment. Non-utility studies quantitatively assessed patients' views, attitudes, satisfaction, or preferences using questionnaires or scales. These studies did not involve utility measurements or responses to decision aids. Patients were asked to rate the desirability or aversiveness of specific outcomes. From the search, 17 studies were included that provided information on various STIs, with many data points informing syphilis-specific evidence. Resource use data were obtained from the published literature, focusing on the direct costs of medications. Based on the GDG's list of potential treatments, the cost associated with each alternative was estimated. This estimate included only the market price of the medication and excluded costs for other resources, such as syringes, injection time, or needle disposal. Data were presented in a structured format, including treatment type, daily dose, treatment duration, cost per dose, total cost for the full treatment course, and 25% of procurement costs as defined by the 2014 Management Sciences for Health (MSH) International Drug Price Indicator Guide. The final price for a full treatment course was calculated by multiplying the number of doses per day by the number of treatment days, plus 25% of procurement costs. Unit prices were obtained from median prices listed in the 2014 MSH guide and other online sources. Calculations were only made when dosage information matched the data of interest. No assumptions were made about hypothetical packaging costs not listed in the directory. Major medical databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, were searched for economic evaluations and technology assessment reports from January 2005 to July 2015. During the screening of treatment effect studies, two investigators also identified studies relevant to costs. However, no studies were found on resource use related to syphilis treatment. The GRADE approach was used to assess the quality of evidence for treatment interventions. This method evaluates evidence based on study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, effect size, dose-response relationships, and other factors that may influence evidence quality. Two investigators independently assessed the quality and certainty of the evidence using GRADE. Evidence profiles for each recommendation, including critical and important outcomes, relative and absolute effects, and evidence quality, were made available in Web Annex D. In October 2015, the GDG convened to develop recommendations. The meeting was co-chaired by experts in GRADE methodology and clinical syphilis management. Methodologists presented evidence profiles and evidence-to-decision frameworks. The GDG discussed each GRADE criterion and determined which intervention was preferred. Final decisions and guideline recommendations were developed through consensus facilitated by the chairpersons. Disagreements on criteria were documented in the evidence-to-decision framework. If disagreements arose regarding final recommendations, the GDG planned to vote and record the results. However, no disagreements occurred, so no votes were taken or reported. The GDG issued strong or conditional recommendations for or against each intervention and provided remarks on special circumstances. Research implications were also developed based on identified evidence gaps. Following the meeting, recommendations were finalized via teleconference, and final approval was obtained electronically from GDG members. All decisions and discussions for each recommendation are documented in the evidence-to-decision frameworks available in Web Annex D.
